title: Chapter V
focus: horror at the moment of creation

teacherSummary.text: On a dreary November night, the creature opens its 'dull yellow eye.' Horrified by its appearance, Victor flees, dreams of Elizabeth turning into his mother's corpse, and wakes to see the creature reaching toward him. He runs into the street, meets Clerval, and collapses into a long fever, nursed by Henry.

vocabulary.definition: To move with a violent, irregular action
vocabulary.context: “Compose yourself,” said Clerval, who observed my change of colour, “I will not mention it, if it agitates you; but your father and cousin would be very happy if they received a letter from you in your own handwriting.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “agitate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To beat rapidly and more strongly than usual
vocabulary.context: My heart palpitated in the sickness of fear; and I hurried on with irregular steps, not daring to look about me:—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “palpitate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To pour in, as a liquid
vocabulary.context: I had worked hard for nearly two years, for the sole purpose of infusing life into an inanimate body.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “infuse”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To slip or slide back, in a literal sense
vocabulary.context: By very slow degrees, and with frequent relapses, that alarmed and grieved my friend, I recovered.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “relapse”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A condition of the body, or mind, when its voluntary functions are performed with difficulty, and only by a strong…
vocabulary.context: At length lassitude succeeded to the tumult I had before endured; and I threw myself on the bed in my clothes, endeavouring to seek a few moments of forgetfulness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “lassitude”: -ude (Latin -udo, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The recovery of heath and strength after disease
vocabulary.context: It was a divine spring; and the season contributed greatly to my convalescence.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “convalescence”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ence (Latin -entia, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To spring down, get down, or descend, as from on horseback or from a carriage
vocabulary.context: “My dear Frankenstein,” exclaimed he, “how glad I am to see you! how fortunate that you should be here at the very moment of my alighting!”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “alight”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: But I was in reality very ill; and surely nothing but the unbounded and unremitting attentions of my friend could have restored me to life.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unbounded”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being wild
vocabulary.context: Clerval at first attributed my unusual spirits to joy on his arrival; but when he observed me more attentively, he saw a wildness in my eyes for which he could not account; and my loud, unrestrained, heartless laughter, frightened and astonished him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “wildness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Unable to endure the aspect of the being I had created, I rushed out of the room, and continued a long time traversing my bedchamber, unable to compose my mind to sleep.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “bedchamber”: be- (Old English be-, "thoroughly, about") + -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Gothic novels used darkness, storms and nightmares to produce dread. The quoted lines from Coleridge's 'Ancient Mariner' reinforce Victor's guilt.

significance: The irony is sharp: the being Victor labored to make is abandoned within minutes. The creature's outstretched hand may be a gesture of affection that Victor reads as threat.
discussionQuestions: Was the creature's first gesture threatening or loving? Use evidence.
Where does imagery appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the costs of unchecked ambition?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter V,” how does Shelley show horror at the moment of creation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the imagery you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter V develops the idea of horror at the moment of creation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses imagery in Chapter V to complicate the reader's understanding of horror at the moment of creation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter V within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of horror at the moment of creation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter V as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of horror at the moment of creation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Was the creature's first gesture threatening or loving? Use evidence. No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are agitates, palpitated, infusing, relapses, lassitude. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““Compose yourself,” said Clerval, who observed my change of colour, “I will not mention it, if it agitates you; but your father and cousin would be very happy if they received a letter from you in your own handwriting.” Webster's says: To move with a violent, irregular action. Now the word history: “agitate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “palpitate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “infuse”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Gothic novels used darkness, storms and nightmares to produce dread. The quoted lines from Coleridge's 'Ancient Mariner' reinforce Victor's guilt. Why does this chapter matter? The irony is sharp: the being Victor labored to make is abandoned within minutes. The creature's outstretched hand may be a gesture of affection that Victor reads as threat. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for imagery.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see imagery, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to horror at the moment of creation.

segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of imagery. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
